architecture.approach: Layered per the project constitution: router files declare the path, the express-validator chain and requirePermission('<area>:<action>'); controllers orchestrate and call pure helpers for every rule that needs neither HTTP nor the database (taskGraph, taskQuery, taskNumbers, recurrence, customFields, workflow); Mongoose models persist and own the schema-level limits. The workspace serves the same router twice - /api/workspaces/:slug/tasks directly and /api/tasks as an alias that resolves the active workspace and re-dispatches into the same router - so permissions, validation and responses cannot drift apart. On the client one feature module owns everything: tasksApi is the only place that talks to the API, useTasks is the single source of truth with optimistic updates and a delete undo window, and pure rules (date, filters, taskForm, taskKey, subtasks) live in lib/ with Jest tests.

dataModel.flowDescription: GET /tasks aggregates the workspace's tasks with the filter built by taskQuery.buildTaskFilter, adds the priority rank, sorts (createdAt, deadline, priority or position) and populates only public user fields. A write goes: validate the body -> apply the rules (dates, dependencies, assignees, parent/epic/release/sprint, stage from the workflow, custom values) -> reserve a task number if needed -> save -> record activity -> notify assignees and watchers -> answer with the populated task. Only the fields in EDITABLE_FIELDS are ever set from a request, and every query is scoped to req.workspace._id. Completion of a recurring task additionally creates the next occurrence and clears the rule on the completed one, and deleting a task runs the shared cascade (subtasks, GridFS files, dependencies, relations, epics, time entries).

securityConsiderations.description: Every task query and write is filtered by req.workspace._id, which requirePermission derives from the :slug in the URL, so a member of another workspace cannot reach the data even with a valid task id (a foreign id answers 404 rather than leaking that the task exists).

tasks:read, tasks:write and tasks:delete are enforced by the route middleware from server/src/config/permissions.ts; the only per-item checks left in the controllers compare the stored owner (comment author, attachment uploader, task owner) with req.user._id. Public user fields are limited to name and avatarUrl, so no email, hash or token is ever returned with a task.

Deadlines and start dates are validated as ISO 8601 by express-validator and stored as dates; the client only ever renders the calendar day through lib/date.ts, which avoids timezone shifts that would silently move a task to another day.

performanceConsiderations.strategy: Task numbers come from a single atomic $inc on the workspace document, so concurrent creates cannot collide or deadlock; backfilling is one bulkWrite with an idempotent filter (number does not exist).

The list is one aggregation over an index-prefixed workspace filter, and the same list is reused by every view through a shared query cache on the client, so switching views and revisiting a workspace costs no extra request.

Drag-heavy interactions send small PATCH bodies (position, stage/status) instead of whole tasks, and the rate limiter keeps a separate budget for the live-update polls so board traffic does not lock the API for a team behind one IP.

risks.description: The delete and update cascades touch several collections, so a partial failure could leave a dependency or relation pointing at a task that no longer exists.
risks.mitigation: One shared cleanUpRemovedTasks routine, $pull-based updates that are safe to repeat, and integration tests (server/src/__integration__/tasks.test.ts, relations.test.ts) that assert the state after a delete.

risks.description: Two ways into the same router (/api/tasks alias and /api/workspaces/:slug/tasks) could drift in behaviour.
risks.mitigation: The alias only resolves the slug and re-dispatches to the same router, so permissions, validation and responses are literally the same code.

risks.description: Client-side mirroring of server rules (applyPatch, matchesFilters, missingRequired) can fall behind the API.
risks.mitigation: The mirrors live in lib/ with unit tests next to the server's own tests, and any rejected write rolls back and surfaces the API message instead of silently diverging.
